read.sections.0.heading.source: New machines have changed work before
read.sections.0.heading.back: New machines have changed work before

read.sections.0.text.source: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in cloth factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as Luddites, broke machines in protest, because the machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. Instead, a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That was one machine in one country, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as Luddites, broke machines in protest, because the machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, ATMs slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, the workers who handle money at the counter, to disappear. Instead, a study in 2015 found the number of tellers stayed about the same, and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That is only one machine in one country, so it can't tell us what AI will do.

read.sections.1.text.source: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work, but the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, studied AI tools that write and make things. Its researchers scored about 30,000 tasks for how much of each one these tools could do. They found that about one in four of the world's jobs has some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type in data, have the most. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. It is not a count of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most jobs are made up of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets began to be used on office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work, but the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for matters of work, studied AI tools that write and produce things. Its researchers gave a score to about 30,000 tasks, by how far these tools could do each task. They found that about one in four jobs in the world has some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type data, have the highest exposure. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. This is not a count of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group for work studied AI that writes and makes things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About one in four jobs has some exposure to these tools. That means the tools could do some of the tasks. Office jobs have the most. This is not a count of lost jobs. Most of these jobs will likely change, not disappear.

read.sections.2.text.source: The same change can affect people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, against about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's are in the most exposed group. Change can be uneven inside one office too. In the made-up town of Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third lost her work. The ILO says talks between workers, employers and governments can help to manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
read.sections.2.text.back: The same change can affect different people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, against about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's jobs are in the most exposed group. Change can also be unequal inside one office. In Millbrook, a made-up town, the water office now works faster. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third clerk lost her work. The ILO says discussions between workers, employers and governments can help manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
read.sections.2.text.note: "talks between workers, employers and governments" (the ILO's social dialogue) is "perbincangan" (discussions); "rundingan" (negotiations) is an option for reviewers.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Change can affect people in different ways. The ILO found more exposure in richer countries. There, about one in three jobs has some. In the poorest countries, it is about one in ten. In richer countries, more women's jobs than men's are very exposed. In made-up Millbrook, the water office works faster now. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. Workers, employers and leaders can plan these changes together, the ILO says.

write.example.source: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. The task that changed was typing up forms, because an AI tool now reads most of them. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work moved towards helping people. It is also unlike them, because one clerk lost her job, while the number of tellers did not fall.

watch.summary.source: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
watch.summary.back: This video asks whether machines and AI will take people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. This happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology creates some new jobs, such as building and repairing machines. Technology also makes goods cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and all those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because AI can do many kinds of work. This video says the bigger question may be who profits. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.

educatorNotes.0.source: One estimate in learner text, on purpose: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek and others, 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK; ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks for how far generative AI could do them. 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations with some exposure (34% in high-income countries, 11% in low-income ones); 3.3% are in the most exposed group, mostly clerical jobs such as data entry clerks and typists; in high-income countries that group is 9.6% of women's jobs and 3.5% of men's. The ILO says the figures reflect potential exposure, an upper limit, not the actual effect on employment; it expects most jobs to be transformed rather than made redundant, though efficiency gains could still reduce demand for workers. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: almost 40% of jobs exposed to AI in general), cover a wider set of technologies and use another method, so they can't be set beside the ILO's number; the lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015), and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015); each is one past case, not a forecast for AI.

educatorNotes.1.source: The Speak discussion has no single right answer. Ideas might include retraining the clerk for another task, moving more slowly, or sharing the remaining work; ask who would have to agree (the employer, the workers, a union or the government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between them. A teacher could add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's own job.
